topics.title: AWS Regions and how to choose one

kcs.statement: An AWS Region is a separate geographic area made up of multiple isolated Availability Zones, and most AWS resources are created in and scoped to one Region.

The four factors for choosing a Region are compliance and data-residency rules, proximity to users (latency), which services and features are available there, and price, which differs between Regions.
Data stored in a Region stays in that Region unless the customer explicitly copies or moves it elsewhere, so picking a Region inside a country is how data-residency laws are met.

serves.reason: Every placement decision starts with choosing a Region for latency, compliance, service availability or price

topics.title: Availability Zones: isolated data centers in a Region

kcs.statement: An Availability Zone is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking and connectivity, located inside a Region.
Availability Zones in a Region are physically separated by a meaningful distance and do not share single points of failure, so a fire, flood or power cut in one should not take down another.
Availability Zones in the same Region are joined by redundant, low-latency, high-bandwidth private links, which makes synchronous replication between them practical.

serves.reason: Choosing AZs versus Regions for availability needs a precise idea of what an AZ isolates

requires.reason: An AZ is defined as a part of a Region

topics.title: High availability with multiple AZs and Regions

kcs.statement: Running an application's resources in at least two Availability Zones keeps it available when one AZ fails, and is the standard way to achieve high availability within a Region.
A second Region is used for disaster recovery from a Region-wide outage, for lower latency to users on another continent, or to meet residency rules in several countries.
Multi-Region designs add cost and complexity (cross-Region replication and data transfer), so multi-AZ is the default for availability and multi-Region is chosen only when a requirement demands it.

requires.reason: Multi-AZ resilience depends on knowing that AZs are isolated failure domains

topics.title: Edge locations: content close to users

kcs.statement: Edge locations are AWS sites in many more cities than there are Regions, used by CloudFront to cache content and by Route 53 and Global Accelerator to answer and route traffic close to users.
Edge locations do not host general workloads such as EC2 instances or databases; the origin stays in a Region and the edge reduces latency for delivering content to users.

requires.reason: Edge locations are explained in contrast to Regions, where the origin lives

topics.title: Local Zones, Wavelength and Outposts

kcs.statement: A Local Zone extends a Region into a large metro area by placing AWS compute and storage close to end users there, for single-digit-millisecond latency (for example, media rendering or real-time gaming).
A Wavelength Zone embeds AWS compute and storage inside a telecom provider's 5G network, so mobile and connected devices reach applications without traffic leaving the carrier network.

AWS Outposts are AWS-managed racks installed in the customer's own data center that run AWS services on premises, used for very low latency to local systems, local data processing or data that must stay on site.

Placement rule: users concentrated in one city needing ultra-low latency means Local Zone, 5G mobile devices means Wavelength, and workloads that must run in the customer's own facility means Outposts.

topics.title: Choosing where to run: a placement guide

kcs.statement: For a latency requirement, choose the Region closest to users, add edge locations for cacheable content, and use Local Zones or Wavelength only when single-digit-millisecond latency is required.
For an availability requirement, spread resources across Availability Zones; add a second Region only when the requirement names a regional disaster or global users.
Global infrastructure lets a company launch in a new country in minutes by choosing an existing Region instead of building a data center, which is the speed-of-deployment and global-reach benefit.

topics.title: Shared responsibility: security of vs in the cloud

kcs.statement: AWS is responsible for security of the cloud: the physical data centers, hardware, global network and the host and virtualization layer that run AWS services.

The customer is responsible for security in the cloud: what it puts on and configures in AWS, such as guest operating systems on IaaS, application code, firewall settings like security groups, and encryption choices.
For every service type the customer keeps responsibility for its own data, how it is classified, and which identities can access it.

serves.reason: Sorting security tasks between AWS and the customer is the core of the o3 product

topics.title: Shared responsibility for EC2, RDS and Lambda

kcs.statement: With EC2, an IaaS service, the customer patches the guest operating system and applications and configures security groups, while AWS secures the physical host and hypervisor.

With Amazon RDS, a managed database, AWS patches the database engine and underlying operating system, while the customer manages database users and permissions, network access rules, encryption settings and public accessibility.
With AWS Lambda, AWS manages the servers, operating system and runtime patching, while the customer is responsible for function code, its dependencies, its IAM permissions and its data.

requires.reason: Per-service splits apply the of/in division

topics.title: Shared and inherited controls

kcs.statement: Patch management, configuration management, and awareness and training are shared controls: AWS performs them for its infrastructure and the customer performs them for its own guest systems, applications and staff.
Physical and environmental controls are inherited controls: the customer relies entirely on AWS for them and can cite AWS's audits of them in its own compliance work.

topics.title: AWS accounts and the root user

kcs.statement: An AWS account is a container for resources that acts as a billing and security boundary: by default resources in one account are isolated from other accounts.
The root user is the identity created with the account's sign-up email address and has full access to every resource and the billing settings, which IAM policies cannot restrict.
Some tasks require the root user, including changing the root email or password, closing the account, restoring an IAM administrator's lost permissions, and enabling MFA Delete on an S3 bucket.

serves.reason: Recognising root-only tasks and the root user's power underpins the access-management part of o3

topics.title: Protecting the root user with MFA

kcs.statement: Multi-factor authentication requires a second factor in addition to the password, such as a code from a virtual authenticator app, a FIDO2 passkey or security key, or a hardware TOTP token.
To protect the root user: enable MFA, set a strong password, do not create root access keys (delete any that exist), and sign in as root only for root-only tasks.
MFA should be enabled for every human identity with console access, not only the root user, because it stops a stolen password alone from granting access.

requires.reason: Root protection presupposes knowing what the root user is and can do

topics.title: IAM users and groups

kcs.statement: IAM is a global, no-cost AWS service that controls who can sign in to an account (authentication) and what they are allowed to do (authorization).
An IAM user is a long-term identity for one person or application with its own credentials, and a newly created IAM user has no permissions until some are granted.
An IAM group is a collection of IAM users that share the permissions attached to the group; a user can belong to several groups, but groups cannot contain other groups.

requires.reason: IAM users are introduced as the everyday alternative to the root user

topics.title: IAM policies: JSON permissions and evaluation

kcs.statement: An IAM policy is a JSON document whose statements each give an Effect (Allow or Deny), the Actions, the Resources, and optional Conditions.
Identity-based policies attach to users, groups or roles, while resource-based policies attach to a resource such as an S3 bucket and name which principals may access it.
IAM denies every request by default, an explicit Allow grants access, and an explicit Deny in any applicable policy overrides any Allow.

serves.reason: Predicting whether a request is allowed relies on policy structure and evaluation

topics.title: IAM roles and temporary credentials

kcs.statement: An IAM role is an identity with permissions but no long-term password or access keys, assumed by a trusted entity such as an AWS service, an IAM user, another account or a federated user.
Assuming a role returns temporary credentials from AWS Security Token Service (STS) that expire automatically after a set duration.
An application running on EC2 should get its AWS permissions from a role attached to the instance rather than from access keys stored on the server.

serves.reason: Roles are the IAM feature that answers 'give a service or another account access securely'

requires.reason: A role's permissions are expressed as attached policies

topics.title: Least privilege and IAM best practices

kcs.statement: The principle of least privilege means granting an identity only the permissions it needs for its task, starting from none and adding more only when required.
IAM best practice is to assign permissions through groups, use roles for applications and cross-account access, require MFA, rotate long-term credentials, and never share credentials.

The IAM credential report lists every user and the status of their passwords, access keys and MFA, and IAM access advisor shows which services an identity last used, so unused permissions can be removed.

topics.title: Console, CLI and SDKs: ways to reach AWS

kcs.statement: The AWS Management Console is the browser interface, signed into with a username and password plus MFA, for working with AWS services by point and click.
The AWS CLI and SDKs authenticate programmatic requests with an access key ID and secret access key or with temporary credentials, and these keys must be protected like passwords.
The console, CLI and SDKs all call the same AWS service APIs: the CLI is for commands and scripts in a terminal, and SDKs let application code in languages like Python or Java call AWS.
